options.E: None of the above / More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Constitutional experts generally classify constitutions into two main types—(i) Federal and (ii) Unitary. A unitary constitution is one in which all powers are vested in a single government, usually the central government. In such a system, provinces/states remain subordinate to the centre. In contrast, a federal constitution divides powers between the Centre and the States, and both governments function independently within their respective spheres. There has been considerable difference of opinion among jurists regarding the nature of the Indian Constitution. According to the Constitution-makers, it is federal; however, Prof. Jennings objected to calling it fully federal. Prof. K. C. Wheare described it as a quasi-federal constitution, or as a unitary constitution with federal features playing a supporting role. Jennings also pointed out a strong tendency towards centralization in the Indian Constitution. Therefore, from the above analysis, we can say that the Indian Constitution is neither purely federal nor purely unitary; rather, it is federal in structure but unitary in spirit.

questions.q: The power to recruit the Secretarial staff of the House of the People is vested in:
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

questions.explanation: At the administrative level, the authority to issue appointment orders for the Lok Sabha Secretariat staff lies with the Speaker (Speaker of the Lok Sabha), while the constitutional rule-making power for this entire framework, under Article 98(3), lies with the President, who, after consultation with the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, makes rules for regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of the Lok Sabha Secretariat staff. questions.q: What constitutes the definition of money bill under article 110 of the Indian Constitution?

questions.q: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) is necessary to be laid before the Parliament ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Article 112 of the Indian Constitution relates to the Annual Financial Statement (Budget). Under Article 112(1), the President shall cause to be laid before both Houses of Parliament, in respect of every financial year, a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year, which is called the “Annual Financial Statement” (Budget).

questions.q: By whom are the expenses of the Parliament of India controlled?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More then one of the above

questions.explanation: Parliament is the supreme legislative body of India. The Indian Parliament consists of the President and two Houses—Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and Lok Sabha (House of the People). The President has the power to summon or prorogue either House of Parliament, and to dissolve the Lok Sabha. Financial authorisation relating to the Consolidated Fund of India, the Contingency Fund of India and the Public Account of India is given only by Parliament. Therefore, the expenditure of the Parliament of India is controlled by Parliament itself.

questions.q: What is the object of “cut motion” in Parliament ?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: To move a proposal to reduce expenditure in the budget proposals
options.B: To restrict day-to-day financial expenditure of the government
options.C: To restrict grants from consolidated fund of India
options.D: To restrict the grants of the Government

questions.explanation: A proposal moved in the lower House (Lok Sabha) to modify the Demands for Grants of the Union Budget is called a Cut Motion. Through it, the Demands for Grants presented for expenditure in the budget are considered improper, and a proposal is brought to reduce them. Cut Motions are of three types—Policy Cut Motion, Token Cut Motion and Economy Cut Motion.

questions.q: A seat of an M.P. can be declared vacant if he absents himself from the house for a continuous period of –
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

However, in computing this period, no account shall be taken of any period during which the House is prorogued or is adjourned for more than four consecutive days.

questions.q: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha enjoys

options.B: The right to vote like other members of the House
options.C: Two votes - one in ordinary course and the other in case of a tie

questions.explanation: Under Article 100(1), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha does not vote in the first instance on any matter; but if the votes are equally divided, the Speaker has and exercises a casting vote. Further, under Article 96(1), when a resolution for the Speaker’s removal is under consideration in the Lok Sabha, the Speaker shall not preside even if present; and under Article 96(2), in that situation, the Speaker shall have the right to vote in the first instance on that resolution, but shall not have the right to exercise a casting vote in case of equality of votes. On this basis, option (c) may also appear correct; however, option (a) is the more precise answer.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution restrict a Member of Parliament to hold the office of profit ?

questions.explanation: Article 102 (1) (a) of the Constitution bars a Member of Parliament from holding an office of profit. Under this Article, a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament if he holds any office of profit under the Government of India or the Government of any State, other than an office declared by Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder.

questions.q: Consider the following statements: 1. The summoning of the House means convocation 2. Prorogation ends a session 3. Dissolution terminates a House 4. Prorogation of a session can be effected by the leader of the House alone Out of these which is not true?
questions.question_type: Multiple Statements — Incorrect Combination by Code
questions.explanation: This question relates to the major procedures of the Indian Parliament/Legislature—Summoning, Adjournment, Prorogation, and Dissolution. Adjournment is done by the Presiding Officer/Speaker/Chairman (or the person acting as such), whereas prorogation is done by the President/Governor. Also, by adjournment, the House is adjourned for a definite or indefinite period; it does not end the session, i. e., it does not amount to prorogation. In fact, prorogation ends a session. Note: In the statement (4) Prorogation of a session can be effected by the leader of the House alone is incorrect. So answer is option (d).

questions.q: Joint Session of both the Houses of Parliament is concerned 1. For the election of the President of India 2. For the election of the vice-President of India 3. To pass the Bill relating to the amendment of Constitution 4. To discuss and pass such a Bill where both Houses have different opinion Select your answer from the following code –
questions.question_type: List and Code — Correct Combination
questions.explanation: According to Article 108 of the Constitution, a joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament is held when there is a disagreement between the two Houses in considering and passing a Bill. The provision of a joint sitting under Article 108 applies only to ordinary Bills; it is not applicable to Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills. Under Article 118(4) (read with the rules made for joint sittings under Article 118(3)), the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the joint sitting. In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides; and if he/she is also absent, the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha presides. The joint sitting is conducted according to the rules for joint sitting made under Article 118(3). The quorum for a joint sitting is one-tenth of the total number of members of both Houses.

questions.q: How many members can the President nominate to the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha respectively?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Quantitative Factual, Single Correct
questions.explanation: Under Article 80, the President may nominate 12 persons to the Rajya Sabha who have special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, and social service. Thus, in the context of the question as asked at that time, the intended answer was option (b). However, after the Constitution (One Hundred and Fourth Amendment) Act, 2019 came into force (25 January 2020), the provision under Article 331 ceased to have effect, and now the President can nominate only 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.

questions.q: What is true about Censure Motion?

questions.q: Vote on Account is meant for -
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: Vote on the report of CAG
options.C: Appropriating funds pending passing of budget
options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India only after the Appropriation Bill is passed. However, if there is a change in the government at the end of the financial year and the new government does not immediately introduce the Appropriation Bill, or if for any other reason money is needed even before the Appropriation Bill is passed, then under Article 116(1)(a) the Lok Sabha can pass a Vote on Account and approve an advance amount for the government. Article 116 also provides that if, in emergency circumstances, the government needs a very large amount of money—such as during war—then the Lok Sabha grants a Vote of Credit, and Parliament authorizes the withdrawal by law.

questions.q: The Public Accounts Committee submits its reports to-
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.B: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha

questions.explanation: The Public Accounts Committee submits its report to the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, and it is presented in the Lok Sabha in the presence of the Speaker. The Public Accounts Committee is a parliamentary committee that exercises control over public expenditure. It consists of 22 members in total—15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha. Its purpose is to bring before the House the misuse and irregularities in public expenditure. It also recommends action against those public authorities who are found responsible for the misuse of public expenditure. The committee examines public expenditure on the basis of the CAG’s report. Generally, it has been the practice (since 1967) to appoint an opposition member of the Lok Sabha as its Chairperson. The Chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee is appointed by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Which of the following is a parliamentary committee relating to delegation of power to make rules and regulations of the executive?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/more than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation is related to the delegated power given to the executive to frame rules and regulations. The function of this parliamentary committee is to examine whether the powers conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parliament—such as making rules, regulations, sub-rules, schemes, or other statutory instruments—are being properly exercised by the executive or not. Both Houses of Parliament have their own Committee on Subordinate Legislation, in which 15 members are nominated from the concerned House by the Speaker/Chairman, as the case may be.

questions.q: By passing, 'Triple Talaq Law' recently, the Parliament of India endorsed which year's ruling of the Supreme Court of India that had made Triple Talaq (Talaq-e- Biddat) as unconstitutional?
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.E: None of the above/More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In Shayara Bano v. Union of India and Others, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court, in a landmark judgment in 2017, held the practice of triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) unconstitutional, declaring it a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. In support of this judgment, the Parliament of India enacted the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, making the practice of triple talaq (instant talaq on the basis of pronouncing talaq three times, including in written and electronic form) legally invalid and unlawful.

questions.q: With reference to the Consumer Disputes Redressal at the district level in India, which one of the following statements is not correct?
questions.question_type: Incorrect Statement — Single Incorrect/Exception

options.A: The District Forum entertains the complaints where the value of goods or services does not exceed rupees fifty lakhs.
options.B: The State Government can establish more than one District Forum in a district if it deems fit.
options.C: One of the members of the District Forum shall be a woman.
options.D: More than one of the above
options.E: None of the above

questions.explanation: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides a three-tier quasi-judicial mechanism for the resolution of consumer disputes, which includes the District Commission, State Commission, and National Commission. Under this Act, the State Government shall establish a District Commission and, if it deems fit, may establish more than one District Commission in a district. The District Commission consists of a President (qualified to be a District Judge) and at least two members; at least one among the President or the members must be a woman (and the minimum age for both the President and members is 35 years). The jurisdiction of the District Commissions includes complaints where the value paid for goods or services does not exceed `50 lakh.

questions.q: Supreme Court in India was established-
questions.question_type: Standard MCQ — Direct Factual/Conceptual, Single Correct

options.A: By an Act of Parliament in 1950

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of India is the highest judicial body under the Constitution of India. Article 124 of the Constitution states that “There shall be a Supreme Court of India.” With the commencement of the Constitution on 26 January 1950, the Supreme Court came into existence. Before shifting in 1958 to its present building on Tilak Marg, New Delhi, it functioned in the Old Parliament House. On 28 January 1950, two days after India became a fully sovereign democratic republic, the Supreme Court was inaugurated. It was inaugurated in the Chamber of Princes in the Old Parliament House, where the Federal Court of India had functioned for 12 years (from 1937 to 1950).

questions.q: Currently, the number of Supreme Court judges is-

options.E: None of the above/More then one of the above

questions.explanation: Article 124 of the Constitution provides for the composition of the Supreme Court and states that it shall consist of a Chief Justice and 7 other judges, and that Parliament may, from time to time, determine the number of judges by law. To fix the number of judges, Parliament enacted the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956, and fixed the number of judges at 10 (excluding the Chief Justice). By amending this Act, the number of judges has been increased from time to time. Under the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019, the present maximum sanctioned strength of judges in the Supreme Court is 33 (excluding the Chief Justice).

questions.q: What is the retirement age of the Judges of the Supreme Court ?

In such a situation, the tenure of State Assemblies will have to be increased or reduced accordingly, and the existing tenure of the Lok Sabha will also have to be adjusted in the same manner. Therefore, for such a system, amendments would be required in Article 83 (Duration of the Houses of Parliament), Article 85 (Sessions of Parliament, prorogation and dissolution), Article 172 (Duration of State Legislatures), Article 174 (Sessions of the State Legislature, prorogation and dissolution), Article 356 (Provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States/President’s Rule in States), etc. It is noteworthy that a high-level committee on “One Nation, One Election” was constituted on 2 September 2023 under the chairmanship of former President Ram Nath Kovind, which submitted its report to President Droupadi Murmu on 14 March 2024.

questions.q: Which of the following are matters on which a constitutional amendment is possible only with the ratification of the legislature of not less than one-half of the states? 1. Election of the President. 2. Representation of States in Parliament. 3. Any of the lists in the 7th Schedule. 4. Abolition of the Legislative Council of a State. Choose the correct answer.
questions.question_type: List and Code — Correct Combination
questions.explanation: The Indian Constitution is flexible and dynamic. As required, it can be amended according to the procedure given in Article 368 of the Constitution. In the Indian Constitution, amendments can be made in three ways— 1. By simple majority—There are some provisions in the Constitution which Parliament can amend by a simple majority. Such amendments are not treated as “amendments of the Constitution” for the purposes of Article 368. For example—changing the names and boundaries of states or creating new states; creating or abolishing Legislative Councils in states; increasing the salaries of the President, Governors, and the judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, etc. These are done by simple majority. 2. By special majority—Under the procedure of Article 368(2), Parliament can amend most Articles of the Constitution by passing a bill in each House by a special majority (i. e., a majority of the total membership of the House and a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting). 3. By special majority and with state ratification— According to the proviso to Article 368(2), there are certain provisions of the Constitution which require, along with Parliament’s special majority, approval by the legislatures of at least half of the states. For example—election of the President and its procedure; extent of the executive power of the Union and the states; provisions relating to the Supreme Court and High Courts; representation of states in Parliament; Parliament’s power and procedure to amend the Constitution; division of legislative powers between the Union and the states and entries in the lists of the Seventh Schedule; provisions relating to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council (Article 279A), etc.
